# Lung cancer

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Pulmonology > Neoplastic lung diseases > Lung cancer*

[Original Article Link](/library/nh07ef)

---

## Summary

<u>Lung</u> cancer is the leading cause of cancer <u>death</u> in the US, accounting for almost a quarter of all cancer-related fatalities; 80–90% of cases can be attributed to smoking. <u>Lung</u> cancer is generally divided into two types: <u>small cell lung cancer</u> (<u>SCLC</u>) and <u>non-small cell lung cancer</u> (<u>NSCLC</u>). <u>SCLC</u> is a single histological category and is characterized by its central location, rapid <u>tumor</u> growth, early <u>metastasis</u>, and association with numerous <u>paraneoplastic syndromes</u>. <u>NSCLC</u> accounts for ∼ 85% of all <u>lung</u> cancers and has multiple histological subtypes including <u>adenocarcinoma</u> and central <u>squamous cell carcinoma</u>. Patients with <u>lung</u> cancer are usually asymptomatic during the early stages of the disease. <u>Lung</u> cancer may be diagnosed after the incidental discovery of a pulmonary <u>nodule</u> on imaging. Late-stage disease can manifest with pulmonary symptoms, extrapulmonary symptoms, <u>paraneoplastic syndromes</u> (e.g., <u>syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion</u>, <u>hypercalcemia</u>), and/or signs of <u>metastatic</u> disease. Patients with <u>lung</u> cancer frequently present with <u>metastasis</u> to the <u>brain</u>, <u>liver</u>, <u>adrenal glands</u>, and/or bones. Evaluation generally begins with CT imaging of the chest and the diagnosis is confirmed with a <u>bronchoscopic</u> or CT-guided <u>biopsy</u>. Patients with no evidence of distant <u>metastases</u> may be eligible for curative surgical resection (with or without adjunct <u>chemotherapy</u>) or <u>radiation therapy</u>. Unfortunately, most patients present with <u>metastatic</u> disease and are, therefore, not eligible for curative resection. These patients often receive palliative <u>chemoradiotherapy</u>. Prognosis is generally poor, with a 5-year survival rate below 20%.

---

## Epidemiology

* <u>Incidence</u> [[1]](/library/MKbMSu)[[2]](/library/LKbwSu)

* Second most common cancer

* Leading cause of cancer <u>death</u> worldwide

* Age: peak <u>incidence</u> at 65–75 years [[1]](/library/MKbMSu)

* Sex [[1]](/library/MKbMSu)
* <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u>

* Except for <u>adenocarcinoma</u>, which is more common in women [[3]](/library/NmX-fA)

* Declining <u>incidence</u> in men

* <u>Mortality rates</u> for men and women are converging [[4]](/library/lmXvfA)

## Etiology

* <u>Tobacco smoking</u> ;  [[5]](/library/LmXwTA)[[6]](/library/TZa6aQ)[[7]](/library/oKb0hu)

* Associated with the development of 80–90% of <u>lung</u> cancers

* The risk of cancer is determined by the number of pack years (quantity of cigarette packs a person smoked per day multiplied by the number of years of cigarette consumption)

* Weaker association with <u>lung adenocarcinoma</u>

* Occupational and environmental exposure to <u>carcinogens</u> [[6]](/library/TZa6aQ)

* <u>Passive smoking</u>

* <u>Radon</u> (2<sup>nd</sup> leading cause of <u>lung</u> cancer) and uranium (radioactively decays into <u>radon</u>)  [[8]](/library/KKbUhu)

* <u>Asbestos</u> [[9]](/library/6Kbjhu)

* Occupational <u>carcinogens</u> (e.g., <u>arsenic</u>, <u>chromium</u>, <u>nickel</u>, <u>beryllium</u>, silica)

* Environmental <u>air pollution</u>

* <u>Family history</u> (genetic predisposition)

* Other <u>risk factors</u>: pulmonary scarring, previous radiation, <u>pulmonary fibrosis</u>, chronic infections (e.g., <u>tuberculosis</u>, <u>HIV</u>) [[10]](/library/J3bsjt)





> [!TIP]
> Smokers exposed to <u>asbestos</u> have a significantly higher risk of developing <u>lung</u> cancer compared to smokers that are not.

> [!NOTE]
> Squamous cell and Small cell <u>lung</u> cancer are both Sentrally located.




> [!NOTE]
> For <u>squamous cell lung cancer</u>, imagine a Squawking Parrot doing Karate in the Center of a Cave under a Bridge while Smoking: Squamous cell, <u>PT</u>HrP → <u>hypercalcemia</u>, <u>Keratin</u> pearls, Central location, Cavitation, intercellular Bridges, Smoking.




> [!NOTE]
> For <u>small cell lung cancer</u>, think of small blue KulChA flatbread In a Synapse: Kulchitsky cells, Chromogranin A, <u>neuron</u>-specific Enolase, Synaptophysin.

### Variants of <u>lung</u> cancer




#### Pancoast tumor [[19]](/library/rKbf3u)[[20]](/library/7Kb43u)




* An apical <u>lung</u> <u>carcinoma</u>

* Located in the superior sulcus of the <u>lung</u> (<u>superior sulcus tumor</u>)

* Predominantly <u>NSCLC</u>

* May lead to the development of Pancoast syndrome: a constellation of symptoms secondary to the <u>mass effect</u> of the <u>tumor</u> on surrounding structures

* Cervical <u>sympathetic ganglion</u> (<u>stellate ganglion</u>): <u>Horner syndrome</u> (<u>ipsilateral</u> <u>miosis</u>, <u>ptosis</u>, and <u>anhidrosis</u>)

* <u>Brachial plexus</u>

* Localized <u>pain</u> in the <u>axilla</u> and shoulder (plexus <u>neuralgia</u>)

* Upper limb motor and sensory deficits (e.g., hand <u>muscle weakness</u> and <u>atrophy</u>)

* <u>Recurrent laryngeal nerve</u>: <u>hoarseness</u>

* <u>Brachiocephalic vein</u>

* Unilateral <u>edema</u> of the arm

* Facial swelling

* <u>Phrenic nerve</u>: <u>paralysis</u> of the hemidiaphragm (visible as elevated hemidiaphragm on <u>chest x-ray</u>)





![Pancoast tumor](media/ifypk0pd59td5nyvmpkcqx38.jpg)

Pancoast tumor

![Pancoast tumor with chest wall extension](media/z1lkpeznt1n5sit5qldhheox.jpg)

Pancoast tumor with chest wall extension

![Horner syndrome](media/tz558qjtjcrvorq91j9d3f8i.jpg)

Horner syndrome




#### <u>Lymphangitic carcinomatosis</u>




* Spread of cancer cells along lymphatic vessels

* On imaging, a streaky-reticular pattern may be observed.

## Clinical features

<u>Symptoms of lung cancer</u> may be related to the local effects of the <u>tumor</u> in the <u>lung</u> or spread of disease beyond the chest. <u>Lung</u> cancer often only becomes symptomatic in late stages, generally affecting prognosis negatively.




### Pulmonary symptoms [[21]](/library/sKbt3u)




* <u>Cough</u>, <u>hemoptysis</u>

* Progressive <u>dyspnea</u>

* <u>Wheezing</u>

* <u>Chest pain</u>





### Extrapulmonary symptoms [[21]](/library/sKbt3u)




* <u>Constitutional symptoms</u> (weight loss, <u>fever</u>, <u>weakness</u>)

* Signs and symptoms of <u>tumor</u> infiltration and/or compression of neighboring structures

* <u>Superior vena cava syndrome</u> (<u>SVC syndrome</u>); : Compression of the <u>superior vena cava</u> impairs the venous backflow to the <u>right atrium</u>, resulting in venous congestion in the head, neck, and upper extremities.

* <u>Hoarseness</u>: <u>paralysis</u> of the <u>recurrent laryngeal nerve</u>  [[21]](/library/sKbt3u)

* <u>Dyspnea</u> and diaphragmatic elevation: <u>paralysis</u> of the <u>phrenic nerve</u>

* Dullness on percussion, reduced breath sounds: <u>malignant pleural effusion</u> on the affected side

* <u>Postobstructive pneumonia</u> (see “<u>Secondary pneumonia</u>”)

* <u>Dysphagia</u>: esophageal compression





> [!TIP]
> Recurrent respiratory infections (e.g., <u>pneumonia</u>) in the same <u>pulmonary region</u> in patients ≥ 40 years old should always raise suspicion for <u>lung</u> cancer.




![Superior vena cava obstruction](media/opvs3v4y64cdto58e13v54ni.jpg)

Superior vena cava obstruction




### Symptoms of <u>metastatic</u> disease




* Over half of all patients diagnosed with <u>lung</u> cancer have <u>metastatic</u> disease at the time of presentation. [[1]](/library/MKbMSu)

* The symptoms of <u>metastatic</u> disease are site-specific

* <u>Brain</u>: <u>headaches</u>, <u>seizures</u>, focal motor deficits, behavioral changes (see “<u>Brain metastases</u>”)

* <u>Liver</u>; : typically asymptomatic, but may manifest with <u>nausea</u>, <u>jaundice</u>, <u>ascites</u> (see “<u>Metastatic liver disease</u>”)

* <u>Adrenal gland</u>: typically asymptomatic

* Bones: bone <u>pain</u>, elevated serum <u>alkaline phosphatase</u> and <u>calcium</u>





> [!NOTE]
> “<u>Lung</u> cancer loves to BLAB:” the most common sites of <u>metastasis</u> from <u>lung</u> cancer are the Brain, Liver, Adrenals, and Bones.




![Most common routes of metastasis with TNM classification](media/fwwecln2pm6hsmumxho29bj2.jpg)

Most common routes of metastasis with TNM classification

## Pathology

### <u>Non-small cell lung cancer</u> [[11]](/library/pKbLhu)




#### <u>Squamous cell carcinoma</u>




* Characteristics

* Solid, <u>epithelial</u> <u>tumor</u>

* Intercellular bridges (<u>desmosomes</u>)

* <u>Keratin pearls</u>

* <u>Immunohistochemical markers</u>: expression of p40, p63, CK5, or CK6 [[29]](/library/wKbhiu)

* Subtypes

* Keratinizing

* Nonkeratinizing

* Basaloid

* <u>Carcinoma in situ</u>





![Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung](media/l678e4gzkm14xfy08f88bist.jpg)

Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung




#### <u>Adenocarcinoma</u> [[14]](/library/HKbK3u)




* Characteristics

* Glandular <u>tumor</u>

* <u>Mucin</u>-producing cells (positive <u>mucin</u> staining)

* <u>Immunohistochemical</u> makers: expression of napsin A and TTF-1

* Historical terminology
* Bronchioloalveolar carcinoma (<u>BAC</u>): obsolete term for well-differentiated, noninvasive <u>adenocarcinomas</u> that grow along the alveolar septa.

* Today, <u>adenocarcinomas of the lung</u> are rather described on a spectrum of lepidic growth.

* Lepidic growth: noninvasive <u>tumor</u> growth at intact <u>alveoli</u>.

* <u>BAC</u> has been replaced by a variety of <u>adenocarcinoma</u> subtypes (see “Preinvasive subtypes” and “Invasive subtypes” below)

* Preinvasive subtypes

* Atypical adenomatous hyperplasia (AAH)

* Atypical pneumocyte growth along alveolar walls without cytological features of <u>carcinoma</u>

* Size: ≤ 5 mm

* Pulmonary adenocarcinoma in situ (formerly <u>BAC</u>)

* Small (≤ 3 cm) <u>nodule</u> with a lepidic growth pattern

* Lacks any component of invasion

* Invasive subtypes (classified according to the predominant histopathological growth pattern)

* Minimally-invasive pulmonary adenocarcinoma (<u>MIA</u>)

* Small (≤ 3 cm) <u>tumor</u> with a predominantly lepidic pattern

* ≤ 5 mm of invasion

* Lepidic-predominant <u>adenocarcinoma</u> (formerly nonmucinous <u>BAC</u>)

* <u>Tumor</u> primarily shows intraalveolar growth

* At least one focus of invasion > 5 mm

* <u>Mucinous</u>-predominant <u>adenocarcinoma</u> (formerly <u>mucinous</u> <u>BAC</u>)

* <u>Goblet cell</u> or columnar cell growth along alveolar septae

* Multiple areas of invasion

* Additional subtypes

* Acinar

* <u>Papillary</u>

* Solid

* Colloid

* Fetal

* <u>Enteric</u>





![Adenocarcinoma of the lung](media/lw3fu3kokwau5g5osm1790u1.jpg)

Adenocarcinoma of the lung




#### <u>Large cell carcinoma</u>




* Poorly differentiated, large polygonal <u>tumor</u> cells (abundant <u>cytoplasm</u>)

* Prominent nucleoli

* Lacks identifiable glandular, squamous, or neuroendocrine elements on microscopy or <u>immunohistochemistry</u>. 
* Definitive diagnosis cannot be made by <u>biopsy</u>, rather it can only be finalized from completely excised surgical specimens.





![Large cell carcinoma of the lung](media/rinhwp0uy17ifbmsp25s8yf6.jpg)

Large cell carcinoma of the lung




### <u>Neuroendocrine neoplasms</u> [[30]](/library/UKbbfu)




#### <u>Small cell lung cancer</u>




* Characteristics

* High number of <u>mitotic figures</u>  [[31]](/library/omX0gA)

* Kulchitsky cells

* Small, dark blue <u>neuroendocrine cells</u>

* <u>Hyperchromatic</u> <u>nuclei</u> (salt and pepper appearance)

* Scarce <u>cytoplasm</u>

* <u>Immunohistochemical markers</u>

* <u>Chromogranin A</u>

* <u>Neuron-specific enolase</u>

* <u>Synaptophysin</u>

* <u>CD56</u> [[32]](/library/9KbNiu)





![Small cell lung carcinoma](media/u98sk45co2nhjvhqs9l2hqoa.jpg)

Small cell lung carcinoma

![Small cell lung carcinoma](media/qzjkhs07l5qm9vzu4odurq9j.jpg)

Small cell lung carcinoma

![Small cell lung cancer](media/o6ayvgx2yq6qxxvwj5i7qe22.jpg)

Small cell lung cancer




#### Large cell <u>neuroendocrine carcinoma</u>




* Cell characteristics

* Large cells with abundant eosinophilic <u>cytoplasm</u> organized in trabecular or palisading patterns

* Coarse and granular nuclear <u>chromatin</u>

* Prominent <u>necrosis</u>

* High number of <u>mitotic figures</u>  [[31]](/library/omX0gA)

* <u>Immunohistochemical markers</u>

* <u>Chromogranin A</u>

* <u>Synaptophysin</u>





#### <u>Lung neuroendocrine tumor</u>




* Typical (low-grade) subtype 

* Polygonal cells arranged in organoid, trabecular, or insular patterns

* Fine <u>chromatin</u> with small nucleoli

* Few <u>mitotic figures</u>  [[31]](/library/omX0gA)

* Atypical (intermediate-grade) subtype 

* Similar to typical subtype

* Diagnosis requires the additional presence of either <u>necrosis</u> or a higher number of <u>mitotic figures</u>  [[31]](/library/omX0gA)

* <u>Immunohistochemical markers</u> 

* <u>Chromogranin A</u>

* <u>Synaptophysin</u>

* <u>CD56</u>

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[33]](/library/KScU0X0)[[34]](/library/6Scj0X0)[[35]](/library/qScC0X0)[[36]](/library/IScYaX0)




* Screening: annual <u>low-dose CT scan</u> in high-risk patients (see “<u>Screening for lung cancer</u>” for specific indications)

* Initial diagnostic steps: depend on clinical presentation (see “<u>Clinical features of lung cancer</u>” and “<u>Red flags for cough</u>”)

* Pulmonary or extrapulmonary symptoms: Obtain <u>laboratory studies</u> and chest imaging to assess for underlying disease.

* Pulmonary <u>nodule</u> found incidentally or upon screening: Obtain a thin-slice CT chest and manage according to findings (see “<u>Solitary pulmonary nodules</u>”).

* Diagnostic confirmation: <u>histopathology</u>

* Obtain samples through <u>biopsies</u> or <u>cytology</u>.

* Establishes a diagnosis of <u>SCLC</u> or <u>NSCLC</u> (see “Pathology”)

* <u>Imaging for lung cancer staging</u>: may include <u>cross-sectional imaging</u> of the head, chest, and abdomen

* Molecular testing: to identify mutations or markers that may guide treatment

* <u>SCLC</u>: not routinely indicated [[33]](/library/KScU0X0)

* <u>NSCLC</u>: Obtain <u>PD-L1</u> and mutation testing in patients with <u>metastatic</u> disease. [[37]](/library/JScs0X0)





> [!TIP]
> Early <u>diagnosis of lung cancer</u> is challenging, as symptoms are usually mild and/or nonspecific until the disease is advanced. [[36]](/library/IScYaX0)




### Initial studies




#### Common <u>laboratory studies</u>  [[33]](/library/KScU0X0)[[34]](/library/6Scj0X0)[[38]](/library/n6b7lu)




* <u>CBC</u>: may detect <u>anemia</u>, <u>neutropenia</u>, and/or <u>thrombocytopenia</u>

* <u>CMP</u>

* <u>Hypercalcemia</u>: may indicate <u>bone metastasis</u> or <u>paraneoplastic syndrome</u>

* Elevated <u>alkaline phosphatase</u>: may indicate bone and/or <u>liver metastasis</u>

* Abnormal <u>liver function test</u>: may indicate <u>liver metastasis</u>

* <u>LDH</u>: possibly elevated  [[39]](/library/jPc_ec0)





#### Imaging [[36]](/library/IScYaX0)[[38]](/library/n6b7lu)[[40]](/library/tScXYX0)




See also “<u>Imaging for lung cancer staging</u>.”




* Modalities

* <u>Chest x-ray</u>: indicated as first-line imaging study [[40]](/library/tScXYX0)

* CT chest: indicated in all patients with an abnormal <u>chest x-ray</u> or suspicion of <u>lung</u> cancer  [[36]](/library/IScYaX0)

* Findings

* Visualization of <u>nodules</u> and/or masses with features suggestive of <u>malignancy</u>, including: ;  [[41]](/library/56bilu)[[42]](/library/66bjNu)

* Irregular margins (i.e., scalloped or spiculated)

* Large size (> 2 cm)

* Upper lobe location

* The absence of calcifications

* See “Management of a <u>solitary pulmonary nodule</u>” for details on features suggestive of <u>malignancy</u>.

* Indirect signs of <u>malignancy</u>  

* <u>Atelectasis</u>

* <u>Postobstructive pneumonia</u>

* <u>Pleural effusion</u> (particularly unilateral)

* <u>Mediastinal widening</u>

* Examples of findings in specific subtypes

* Hazy infiltrates (characteristic of <u>adenocarcinoma</u> in situ) [[43]](/library/KmXUgA)

* Cavitating lesion with <u>air-fluid levels</u> (characteristic of <u>squamous cell carcinoma</u>)





> [!WARNING]
> A normal <u>x-ray</u> does not rule out <u>lung</u> cancer, as 10–20% of patients with <u>lung</u> cancer will not have findings visible on <u>x-ray</u>. [[36]](/library/IScYaX0)[[44]](/library/7Sc4aX0)[[45]](/library/sSctaX0)




> [!TIP]
> Consider an early chest CT for all patients with suspected <u>lung</u> cancer. [[46]](/library/ypbdHu)




![Invasive mucinous-predominant adenocarcinoma simulating pneumonia](media/hxgipgetjogkavmwea1p14g5.jpg)

### Confirmation of diagnosis




Histopathological analysis of tissue <u>biopsies</u> is required to confirm the <u>diagnosis of lung cancer</u>; <u>cytology</u> may be confirmatory in select cases.




* Obtaining samples: Less invasive methods are preferred. [[38]](/library/n6b7lu)[[47]](/library/76b4mu)

* Pulmonary lesions

* Central: <u>bronchoscopy</u> with transbronchial <u>biopsy</u>

* Peripheral: needle <u>aspiration</u> guided by <u>endobronchial ultrasound</u> or CT

* <u>Pleural effusion</u>: <u>thoracocentesis</u> with <u>cytology</u> of the effusion; pleural <u>biopsy</u> if <u>cytology</u> is negative

* <u>Metastasis</u> to other organs (e.g., <u>mediastinum</u>, <u>lymph nodes</u>): percutaneous or surgical <u>biopsy</u>, <u>bone marrow biopsy</u> if there is suspected <u>bone marrow</u> infiltration [[33]](/library/KScU0X0)[[47]](/library/76b4mu)

* Lesions that cannot be accessed using less invasive techniques : <u>mediastinoscopy</u>, <u>anterior</u> mediastinotomy, or <u>VATS</u>

* Findings

* Confirms the diagnosis and identifies the <u>SCLC</u> or <u>NSCLC</u> subtype (e.g., <u>adenocarcinoma</u>, <u>squamous cell carcinoma</u>, <u>large cell carcinoma</u>)

* See “Pathology” for detailed findings in each subtype.





> [!TIP]
> Obtain confirmation of <u>metastatic</u> disease with <u>histopathological studies</u> if feasible. [[47]](/library/76b4mu)




![Malignant bronchial tumor](media/yog97yloo68ypnpmadl6pdah.jpg)

Malignant bronchial tumor

![Lung cancer](media/mj2xj4qijfjvb4fqd1fr36zy.jpg)

Lung cancer




### Advanced studies




Since the majority of patients present with <u>metastatic</u> disease, a complete staging evaluation is required. Molecular testing can identify mutations and markers that help inform treatment selection.




#### Imaging for lung cancer staging [[33]](/library/KScU0X0)[[34]](/library/6Scj0X0)[[37]](/library/JScs0X0)[[40]](/library/tScXYX0)




Obtain <u>cross-sectional imaging</u> of the <u>brain</u>, chest, and abdomen. <u>PET-CT</u> is increasingly used for staging because of its high <u>sensitivity</u> for <u>metastatic</u> disease. See “<u>Lung cancer staging</u>” for interpretation.  [[33]](/library/KScU0X0)[[34]](/library/6Scj0X0)[[37]](/library/JScs0X0)[[40]](/library/tScXYX0)




* CT thorax and abdomen [[33]](/library/KScU0X0)[[34]](/library/6Scj0X0)[[37]](/library/JScs0X0)[[40]](/library/tScXYX0)

* Recommended in all patients

* <u>Metastatic</u> disease is most common in the <u>liver</u> and <u>adrenal glands</u>.

* <u>Brain</u> imaging ;   [[33]](/library/KScU0X0)[[34]](/library/6Scj0X0)[[40]](/library/tScXYX0)

* <u>MRI</u> <u>brain</u> with <u>gadolinium</u> <u>enhancement</u>: preferred

* CT <u>brain</u> with contrast: alternative

* <u>PET-CT</u> [[33]](/library/KScU0X0)[[34]](/library/6Scj0X0)[[37]](/library/JScs0X0)

* Indicated for the assessment of thoracic and abdominal <u>metastases</u> in <u>NSCLC</u>; may be used in <u>SCLC</u>

* Preferred method to assess <u>bone metastases</u> in all subtypes

* May prevent unnecessary invasive procedures by demonstrating <u>metastatic</u> disease that was occult on other imaging [[40]](/library/tScXYX0)[[48]](/library/J6bsNu)[[49]](/library/r6bfmu)





> [!TIP]
> <u>PET-CT</u> is the most sensitive imaging modality for detecting <u>mediastinal</u> <u>metastases</u>, <u>lymph node</u> involvement, and extrathoracic <u>metastases</u> including <u>adrenal</u>, <u>liver</u>, and bone. [[33]](/library/KScU0X0)[[34]](/library/6Scj0X0)[[37]](/library/JScs0X0)[[40]](/library/tScXYX0)




> [!TIP]
> All metabolically active lesions suspicious for <u>malignancy</u> should undergo <u>biopsy</u> or excision for diagnostic confirmation.

Enlarged lymph nodes in lung cancer

Cerebral metastasis in lung carcinoma 2/2

![Cerebral metastasis in lung carcinoma 1/2](media/wf4ryph9og1zms46cgljg0fx.jpg)

Cerebral metastasis in lung carcinoma 1/2




#### <u>Molecular diagnostics</u> [[37]](/library/JScs0X0)




Molecular testing may provide guidance for the therapy of <u>SCLC</u>, but it is considered mandatory for patients with advanced or <u>metastatic</u> <u>NSCLC</u> as the presence of certain biomarkers modifies therapy. [[50]](/library/Z3cZSX0)




* <u>Genetic testing</u>: next-generation sequencing (entire <u>genome</u>) or <u>RT-PCR</u> for specific mutations [[37]](/library/JScs0X0)

* Indications: patients with advanced or <u>metastatic</u> <u>NSCLC</u>  and nonsmokers with <u>SCLC</u> [[37]](/library/JScs0X0)[[50]](/library/Z3cZSX0)[[51]](/library/s6btmu)

* Goal: to identify oncogenic mutations that may be therapeutically targeted

* Recommended biomarkers

* <u>Epidermal growth factor receptor</u> (<u>EGFR</u>) mutations

* <u>Anaplastic lymphoma kinase</u> (<u>ALK</u>) fusions

* c-<u>ROS</u> <u>oncogene</u> 1 (ROS1) rearrangements

* <u>Immunohistochemistry</u>: programmed death-ligand 1 (<u>PD-L1</u>) testing

* Description: <u>PD-L1</u> is a coregulatory molecule expressed on <u>tumor</u> cells that inhibits <u>T-cell</u> mediated <u>death</u>; <u>cytotoxic T cells</u> express <u>PD-1</u> (a negative regulator) that binds <u>PD-L1</u>.

* Indication: patients with advanced or <u>metastatic</u> <u>NSCLC</u>

* Goal: to identify patients who may respond to <u>immune checkpoint inhibitors</u> [[50]](/library/Z3cZSX0)

---

## Treatment

### Overview




* Management is determined by the type of <u>lung</u> cancer and the stage at presentation.

* If available, multidisciplinary <u>tumor board</u> involvement is recommended in the care of all patients with <u>lung</u> cancer.  [[37]](/library/JScs0X0)

* Early implementation of <u>palliative care</u> measures improves the patient's quality of life and may prolong survival. [[45]](/library/sSctaX0)





> [!TIP]
> The majority of <u>lung</u> cancers are diagnosed at an advanced stage and treatment is largely palliative, not curative. [[34]](/library/6Scj0X0)




| <br>Overview of the <u>treatment of lung cancer</u> [[33]](/library/KScU0X0)[[34]](/library/6Scj0X0)[[37]](/library/JScs0X0)<br> |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cancer type | <u>Tumor stage</u> |  | Treatment approach | Typical treatment regimen |
| <u>NSCLC</u> | Stage I–<u>IIA</u> | No <u>metastases</u> | <br>* Curative<br><br> | <br><br>* Preferred: surgical resection with or without <u>chemotherapy</u>  [[34]](/library/6Scj0X0)[[54]](/library/jqb_yu)[[55]](/library/PqbWAu)<br><br>* Nonsurgical candidates (e.g., those with inoperable disease or significant comorbidities): <u>radiotherapy</u>, e.g., <u>stereotactic radiotherapy</u> [[34]](/library/6Scj0X0)<br><br><br> |
| Stage <u>IIB</u>–IIIC | <br><br>* Preferred: surgical resection plus <u>chemotherapy</u><br><br>* Nonsurgical candidates (e.g., those with inoperable disease or significant comorbidities): <u>chemotherapy</u> plus <u>radiation therapy</u>; possibly adjuvant immunotherapy [[50]](/library/Z3cZSX0)<br><br><br> |  |  |  |
| Stage <u>IVA</u>–B | <u>Metastases</u> | <br>* Palliative<br><br> | <br><br>* Targetable mutation present: molecular <u>targeted therapy</u>  [[37]](/library/JScs0X0)<br><br>* No targetable mutation: <u>chemotherapy</u> and/or immunotherapy  [[37]](/library/JScs0X0)<br><br><br> |  |
| <u>SCLC</u> | Limited stage |  | <br>* Curative<br><br> | <br><br>* Stage I–II and N0: Consider surgical resection.  [[33]](/library/KScU0X0)<br><br>* All patients<br><br>* Systemic therapy and concurrent <u>radiotherapy</u><br><br>* Consider prophylactic <u>cranial</u> <u>irradiation</u> (<u>PCI</u>)  [[33]](/library/KScU0X0)<br><br><br> |
| Extensive stage |  | <br>* Palliative<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Chemotherapy</u> with or without immunotherapy<br><br>* Consider <u>PCI</u> or <u>MRI</u> surveillance.  [[33]](/library/KScU0X0)<br><br><br> |  |





> [!TIP]
> Although <u>SCLC</u> generally has a good initial <u>response to chemotherapy</u>, most patients have a recurrence within 6 months. [[33]](/library/KScU0X0)




### Medical therapy




* <u>Chemotherapy</u>

* Indication: most <u>lung</u> cancers

* Commonly used agents: <u>cisplatin</u> plus a second agent (e.g., <u>etoposide</u>) [[34]](/library/6Scj0X0)

* <u>Targeted therapy</u>

* Indication: advanced or <u>metastatic</u> <u>NSCLC</u> with a demonstrated oncogenic mutation  [[34]](/library/6Scj0X0)[[37]](/library/JScs0X0)[[56]](/library/XMc9M10)

* Mechanism of action: target up-regulated pathways that cause expression of the malignant <u>phenotype</u>

* Commonly used agents: <u>tyrosine kinase inhibitors</u> (<u>TKIs</u>) specific to the mutation OR <u>receptor</u> <u>monoclonal antibodies</u> [[50]](/library/Z3cZSX0)[[57]](/library/d3cohX0)

* <u>EGFR</u> mutation: <u>EGFR</u> <u>TKI</u> (e.g., <u>osimertinib</u>) OR <u>receptor</u> <u>monoclonal antibody</u> (e.g., <u>cetuximab</u>)

* <u>ALK</u> rearrangement: <u>ALK</u> <u>TKI</u> (e.g., <u>alectinib</u>)

* ROS1 rearrangements: <u>crizotinib</u>

* <u>BRAF</u> mutation: <u>dabrafenib</u> PLUS <u>trametinib</u>

* Immunotherapy

* Indications  [[58]](/library/cMcan10)

* Locally advanced or <u>metastatic</u> <u>NSCLC</u>

* Extensive-stage <u>SCLC</u>

* Mechanism of action: alters <u>T-cell</u> function and improves intrinsic <u>cell-mediated immunity</u> [[50]](/library/Z3cZSX0)

* Blocks the <u>PD-L1</u>/<u>PD-1</u> interaction, improving the antitumor effect of <u>endogenous</u> <u>T cells</u>

* Commonly referred to as <u>immune checkpoint inhibitors</u> (<u>ICIs</u>) [[50]](/library/Z3cZSX0)

* Commonly used agents: durvalumab, <u>pembrolizumab</u>, and <u>atezolizumab</u> [[33]](/library/KScU0X0)[[37]](/library/JScs0X0)[[59]](/library/TKb6fu)





### <u>Radiation therapy</u>




<u>Radiation therapy</u> is most commonly used in conjunction with <u>chemotherapy</u> in <u>lung</u> cancer, but it also has other indications in <u>lung</u> cancer management.




* Indications [[33]](/library/KScU0X0)[[34]](/library/6Scj0X0)[[37]](/library/JScs0X0)

* Limited-stage <u>SCLC</u>

* Early or locally advanced (occasionally <u>oligometastatic</u>) <u>NSCLC</u>

* <u>Palliative care</u> for <u>SVC syndrome</u>, painful <u>bone metastases</u>, tissue invasion, and <u>hemoptysis</u>

* To prevent or slow the growth of <u>brain metastases</u> [[33]](/library/KScU0X0)

* Techniques: Depending on the subtype of <u>lung</u> cancer and the therapeutic goal, different techniques are available.

* Concurrent <u>radiotherapy</u> and <u>chemotherapy</u>

* <u>Primary radiotherapy</u> (e.g., <u>stereotactic body radiotherapy</u>)

* Palliative <u>radiotherapy</u> (e.g., <u>external beam radiation</u>, endobronchial <u>brachytherapy</u>)

* Prophylactic intracranial <u>irradiation</u>





### Surgical management [[34]](/library/6Scj0X0)




* Indications

* Stage I–II <u>SCLC</u> and <u>NSCLC</u> without <u>mediastinal lymph node</u> involvement [[33]](/library/KScU0X0)[[34]](/library/6Scj0X0)

* Select patients with stage III <u>NSCLC</u>

* Contraindications to <u>surgery</u>

* Disease characteristics: N3 disease, bulky N2, multiple N2

* Significant comorbidities

* High cardiac risk (based on <u>revised cardiac risk index</u>)

* Critically limited pulmonary reserve [[34]](/library/6Scj0X0)

* <u>Preoperative assessment</u>: Preoperative <u>pulmonary function testing</u> is required prior to <u>lung</u> resection <u>surgery</u> (see “<u>Preoperative cardiac assessment</u>” and “<u>Preoperative pulmonary assessment</u>”). [[60]](/library/qmXCgA)[[61]](/library/ImXYSA)

* A preoperative <u>FEV<sub>1</sub></u> < 1.5 L and <u>DLCO</u> < 60% predicts a poor outcome after <u>lobectomy</u>.

* A preoperative <u>FEV<sub>1</sub></u> < 2 L and <u>DLCO</u> < 80% predicts a poor outcome after <u>pneumonectomy</u>.





| <br><u>Lung</u> resection procedures [[60]](/library/qmXCgA)[[61]](/library/ImXYSA)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Type of resection | Features | Indication |
| Sublobar resection | <br><br>* <u>Wedge resection</u> or segmentectomy<br><br>* Low perioperative <u>morbidity</u><br><br>* Preserves <u>lung function</u><br><br>* Small tissue margins  [[34]](/library/6Scj0X0)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Peripherally located tumors < 2–3 cm [[34]](/library/6Scj0X0)<br><br>* Patients unable to tolerate <u>lobectomy</u> [[62]](/library/ljcv0c0)<br><br><br> |
| <u>Lobectomy</u> | <br><br>* Anatomic resection of an entire pulmonary lobe<br><br>* Accompanied by significant loss of postoperative <u>lung function</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Most tumors > 2–3 cm [[62]](/library/ljcv0c0)<br><br> |
| <u>Pneumonectomy</u> | <br><br>* Complete <u>lung</u> resection<br><br>* High perioperative <u>morbidity</u> and mortality<br><br><br> | <br>* Cancer involving the hilum, main <u>bronchi</u>, or a major <u>fissure</u><br><br> |





> [!WARNING]
> Complications are common after <u>surgery</u> for <u>lung</u> cancer. <u>Morbidity</u> and mortality are higher for larger surgeries (e.g., <u>pneumonectomy</u>) and increase in patients with preexisting comorbidities. [[63]](/library/tPcXgc0)[[64]](/library/8PcOgc0)

## Solitary pulmonary nodules

![Evaluation of solitary pulmonary nodules](media/szopa3miu9m80ph1llcnyy53.jpg)

Evaluation of solitary pulmonary nodules




### Definition




A <u>solitary pulmonary nodule</u> (<u>SPN</u>) is a single, well-defined lesion, ≤ 30 mm in diameter, that is completely located in the <u>pulmonary parenchyma</u>.  [[66]](/library/N6b-Ou)




### Initial assessment




* Perform a detailed clinical evaluation.

* Review any previous imaging (if available) to evaluate for changes.

* Obtain a thin-slice CT chest if not already available.

* Identify <u>nodule</u> size, density (solid vs. subsolid), and other characteristics.   [[66]](/library/N6b-Ou)

* Features suggestive of <u>malignancy</u> include irregular margins, larger size, upper lobe location, and subsolid density.

* Features suggestive of other etiologies include calcifications (see “<u>Differential diagnosis of pulmonary nodules</u>”).

* Determine the <u>risk of malignancy of a solitary pulmonary nodule</u>.





> [!TIP]
> A <u>solitary pulmonary nodule</u> identified on <u>CXR</u> in a patient with high-risk features (e.g., advanced age, smoking history) should be evaluated to rule out <u>malignancy</u>.




### Risk of malignancy in solitary pulmonary nodules




The risk of <u>malignancy</u> can be determined by clinical evaluation and/or predictive modeling and helps guide management and follow-up.  [[66]](/library/N6b-Ou)




* The most extensively validated model is the Mayo Clinic model in which 6 predictors of <u>malignancy</u> are combined in a logarithmic equation to calculate the risk.  [[41]](/library/56bilu)

* Risk categories 

* Low: < 5% (typically, patients with low-risk predictors)

* Intermediate: 5–65% (typically, patients with a mixture of high-risk and low-risk predictors)

* High: > 65% (typically, patients with high-risk predictors)





| ‎Predictors of malignancy risk in patients with SPNs [[41]](/library/56bilu)[[65]](/library/l6bvOu)[[66]](/library/N6b-Ou)<br> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | Low-risk | High-risk |
| <u>Patient history</u> | <br>Age  [[65]](/library/l6bvOu)[[66]](/library/N6b-Ou)[[67]](/library/RY1lK20)<br> | <br>* Young (e.g., < 35 years)  [[65]](/library/l6bvOu)<br><br> | <br>* Older (e.g., > 60 years)  [[67]](/library/RY1lK20)<br><br> |
| Smoking history | <br>* None<br><br> | <br>* Heavy use (current or prior)<br><br> |  |
| Prior cancer history | <br>* None<br><br> | <br>* History of extrathoracic cancer<br><br> |  |
| <u>Nodule</u> features | <br>Size  [[65]](/library/l6bvOu)[[66]](/library/N6b-Ou)<br> | <br>* Small (e.g., < 4 mm)<br><br> | <br>* Large (e.g., > 8–10 mm<br><br> |
| Border | <br>* Smooth<br><br> | <br>* Irregular (e.g., scalloped or spiculated)<br><br> |  |
| Location | <br>* Middle or lower lobe<br><br> | <br>* Upper lobe<br><br> |  |





> [!TIP]
> Subsolid <u>nodules</u> are less common than solid <u>nodules</u> and are more likely to be malignant. [[68]](/library/p6bLNu)




> [!WARNING]
> Assume a <u>solitary pulmonary nodule</u> in a patient with current <u>active cancer</u> is <u>metastatic</u> until proven otherwise. [[65]](/library/l6bvOu)




![Solitary Pulmonary Nodule Malignancy Risk](media/m2ryv6v9gkqzh4kwbj3q8v68.jpg)

Solitary Pulmonary Nodule Malignancy Risk




### Management




The following recommendations are consistent with the 2013 CHEST guidelines and the 2017 Fleischner Society guidelines on the evaluation and management of <u>SPNs</u>. [[65]](/library/l6bvOu)[[66]](/library/N6b-Ou)




* Patients with any of the following characteristics should be excluded from this approach and require case-by-case management: [[65]](/library/l6bvOu)

* Age < 35 years

* <u>Immunocompromise</u>

* Active known primary cancer

* Symptomatic patients

* Options typically include <u>biopsy</u>, further imaging, or long-term surveillance with serial imaging.





> [!WARNING]
> For any <u>nodule</u> followed by serial imaging, clear growth or a change in density should prompt evaluation for a <u>biopsy</u> and/or resection. [[66]](/library/N6b-Ou)




#### Solid <u>nodule</u> > 8 mm




* High risk: Obtain a surgical <u>biopsy</u> and start treatment based on the results.

* Intermediate or low risk: Obtain a <u>PET-CT</u> scan.

* Positive <u>PET-CT</u>: Obtain a surgical <u>biopsy</u>.

* Negative <u>PET-CT</u> and intermediate risk: Obtain a <u>nonsurgical biopsy</u>.

* Suspicious findings: Obtain a surgical <u>biopsy</u>.

* Nondiagnostic findings: Start surveillance with serial <u>CT scans</u>.

* Negative <u>PET-CT</u> and low risk: Observe with serial <u>CT scans</u>.  [[66]](/library/N6b-Ou)





#### Solid <u>nodule</u> ≤ 8 mm




* Most patients are assessed with serial <u>CT scans</u>.  [[66]](/library/N6b-Ou)

* Surveillance frequency is determined by the patient's <u>malignancy</u> risk and <u>nodule</u> size.

* Intermediate or high risk

* < 4 mm: Repeat CT at 12 months; if there is no change in size, no further follow-up is needed.

* 4–6 mm: Repeat CT at 6–12 months and 18–24 months.

* 6–8 mm: Repeat CT at 3–6 months, 9–12 months, and 18–24 months.

* Low risk

* < 4 mm: Surveillance is optional.

* 4–6 mm: Repeat CT at 12 months; if there is no change in size, no further follow-up is needed.

* 6–8 mm: Repeat CT at 6–12 months; if the size remains stable, repeat again at 18–24 months.





> [!TIP]
> Solid lesions that decrease in size but do not completely resolve should be followed until no interval growth has been demonstrated over 2 years. [[66]](/library/N6b-Ou)




> [!TIP]
> Surveillance is optional for low-risk patients with a <u>solitary pulmonary nodule</u> < 4 mm in diameter. [[66]](/library/N6b-Ou)




#### Subsolid pulmonary <u>nodule</u>




Assess with serial <u>CT scans</u>. Surveillance frequency is dictated by the appearance and size of the <u>nodule</u>.




* Pure <u>ground-glass opacification</u> 

* ≤ 5 mm: no further evaluation

* > 5 mm: annual CT for 3 years

* > 10 mm: Consider CT at 3 months.

* Partially solid appearance 

* ≤ 8 mm: Observe with serial CT.

* > 8 mm: Repeat CT at 3 months; obtain <u>PET-CT</u> or <u>biopsy</u> if the <u>nodule</u> persists.

## Differential diagnoses

### Differential diagnosis of pulmonary nodules [[69]](/library/jJb_Fu)




| Differential diagnosis | Examples | Features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Primary <u>lung</u> cancer | <br><br>* <u>Squamous cell carcinoma</u><br><br>* <u>Adenocarcinoma</u><br><br>* <u>SCLC</u><br><br>* <u>Large cell carcinoma</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Single central or peripheral <u>nodule</u><br><br>* Irregular margins and/or <u>spicules</u><br><br>* No calcifications or irregular calcifications<br><br>* Size is typically > 2 cm<br><br><br> |
| <br>Lung metastases [[70]](/library/BKbziu)<br> | <br><br>* <u>Breast cancer</u><br><br>* <u>Colorectal cancer</u><br><br>* <u>Renal cell carcinoma</u><br><br>* <u>Prostate cancer</u><br><br>* <u>Bladder cancer</u><br><br>* <u>Melanoma</u><br><br>* <u>Head and neck cancer</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Most commonly multiple pulmonary <u>nodules</u><br><br> |
| <u>Pulmonary neuroendocrine tumor</u> | <br>* <u>Lung neuroendocrine tumor</u><br><br> | <br><br>* If centrally located, endobronchial <u>nodule</u> or perihilar mass  [[71]](/library/yKbdQu)<br><br>* If peripherally located, round or oval opacities<br><br>* Size typically 2–5 cm<br><br><br> |
| <br>Benign lung tumors [[72]](/library/AKbRQu)[[73]](/library/_Kb5Qu)<br> | <br><br>* Pulmonary hamartoma  <br><br>* Fat, fibromyxoid tissue, sometimes <u>smooth muscle</u><br><br>* Predominantly <u>cartilage</u> (may undergo calcification or osseous changes)<br><br>* Disorganized connective and <u>epithelial tissue</u><br><br>* Other tumors (e.g., <u>lipoma</u>, <u>neurofibroma</u>, <u>leiomyoma</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Popcorn calcifications</u><br><br>* Round, well-circumscribed <u>nodules</u>, lobulated by <u>respiratory epithelium</u><br><br>* Size typically 1–3 cm<br><br>* 90% are peripheral, 10% are endobronchial. [[74]](/library/bsbHtE)<br><br><br> |
| Infectious <u>granulomas</u> | <br><br>* <u>Tuberculosis</u><br><br>* <u>Nontuberculous mycobacteria</u><br><br>* <u>Histoplasmosis</u><br><br>* <u>Coccidioidomycosis</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Round, well-defined, calcified <u>nodule</u><br><br>* Most common cause of benign pulmonary <u>nodules</u> (∼ 80%) [[75]](/library/zKbrQu)<br><br><br> |
| Inflammatory conditions | <br><br>* <u>Sarcoidosis</u><br><br>* <u>Granulomatosis with polyangiitis</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Multiple bilateral cavitating nodular lesions [[76]](/library/-KbDQu)<br><br>* Commonly associated with other systemic findings<br><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> Pulmonary <u>nodules</u> are more commonly <u>metastases</u> of other cancers than primary <u>lung</u> cancer.

## Prevention

### <u>Smoking cessation</u> [[79]](/library/Hf1KnT0)[[80]](/library/KvcUae0)




* <u>Smoking cessation</u> can reduce the risk of developing <u>lung</u> cancer by up to 50% after 5–10 years. [[81]](/library/F6bg5u)[[82]](/library/86bO5u)[[83]](/library/JmXsgA)

* After 15–20 years, the risk of <u>lung</u> cancer is the same as that of <u>never smokers</u>. [[81]](/library/F6bg5u)[[82]](/library/86bO5u)[[83]](/library/JmXsgA)

* For further information, see “<u>Tobacco product use and smoking cessation</u>.”





### <u>Lung cancer screening</u> [[84]](/library/JfdsM60)[[85]](/library/2gcTub0)[[86]](/library/pfdLM60)




For follow-up of abnormal <u>lung cancer screening</u> results, see “<u>Solitary pulmonary nodule</u>” and “<u>Diagnostics of lung cancer</u>”.




* Indications

* Age 50–80 years with ≥ 20 <u>pack-year</u> smoking history  [[84]](/library/JfdsM60)[[85]](/library/2gcTub0)[[86]](/library/pfdLM60)[[87]](/library/qfdCM60)

* <u>Screening recommendations</u> for <u>former smokers</u> varies, with some societies recommending limiting screening to individuals who have smoked within the past 15 years.  [[84]](/library/JfdsM60)[[85]](/library/2gcTub0)[[86]](/library/pfdLM60)[[87]](/library/qfdCM60)

* Modality: : <u>low-dose CT scan</u> of the chest without IV contrast [[88]](/library/ofd0M60)

* Frequency

* Annual screening is recommended.

* Discontinue screening if the patient:

* Develops a comorbidity that substantially limits their <u>life expectancy</u>

* Expresses unwillingness to have curative <u>lung</u> <u>surgery</u>

* No longer meets indications for screening  [[85]](/library/2gcTub0)[[86]](/library/pfdLM60)





> [!TIP]
> In the US, <u>lung cancer screening</u> with <u>low-dose CT</u> chest is estimated to reduce <u>lung</u> cancer mortality by up to 20%. [[85]](/library/2gcTub0)
